q: The skipper asks you to name this point of sail for the logbook. What is it?
a: Broad reach
o: Beam reach
Close reach
Run
why: With the wind about 135° off the bow, over the quarter, you are on a broad reach.

q: The helm turns onto this heading. The sails flap and the boat slows to a stop. Why?
a: The boat is pointing into the no-go zone
o: The sheets are pulled in too tight
The wind has suddenly dropped
The genoa has been furled too far
why: No sail can drive the boat within about 45° of the wind: the no-go zone.

q: The skipper asks you to "ease the main". Which line do you let out?
a: The mainsheet
o: The main halyard
The genoa sheet
The genoa furling line
why: The mainsheet sets the angle of the boom; easing it lets the sail out.

q: You are trimming the genoa on a steady reach. How do you find the right setting for the sheet?
a: Ease until the luff just flaps, then pull in enough to stop it
o: Pull in until the sail is hard and flat, then cleat it
Ease until the whole sail flaps, then cleat it there
Pull in until the tell-tales droop, then leave it
why: The best trim is just short of luffing: ease till it flaps, then sheet in a touch.

q: You are trimming the genoa and see this on the tell-tales. What do you do?
a: Pull the sheet in a little
o: Ease the sheet out a little
Leave it: the trim is right
Ease the genoa halyard a little
why: A lifting windward tell-tale means the sail is eased too far: sheet in.

fig.title: Genoa tell-tales
lines: Close reach, helm on a steady course

q: The skipper asks you to sort out the genoa trim. What do you do with the sheet?
a: Ease it a little
o: Pull it in a little
Cleat it and leave it
Let it fly right out
why: A drooping leeward tell-tale means the sail is stalled, sheeted too hard: ease it.

q: In a tack you are on the new genoa sheet. As the genoa blows across, what do you do?
a: Pull the slack in fast by hand, then winch the last part
o: Wait until the sail fills, then start winding
Wait until the old sheet has been coiled
Winch it in from the start, with all turns on
why: Slack comes in fastest by hand before the sail fills; the winch takes the last, loaded part.

q: The helm calls "Ready to gybe". You are on the mainsheet. What do you do?
a: Pull the main in to the centre, then ease it on the new side
o: Let the mainsheet run free so the boom can swing across
Cleat it where it is and keep well clear of the boom
Ease it out further to spill the wind from the sail first
why: Hauling the boom in first keeps its swing short and controlled; then ease it out.

q: The skipper asks you to furl the genoa. What do you do with the furling line and the sheet?
a: Pull the furling line; ease the sheet with some tension
o: Pull the sheet; ease the furling line slowly
Pull the furling line; let the sheet fly free
Pull the genoa halyard; ease the sheet
why: Light tension on the sheet rolls the sail up tightly and stops it flogging.

q: You are unfurling the genoa in a fresh breeze. What do you do with the furling line?
a: Ease it out under control, with a turn round a winch
o: Let it go completely so the sail opens fast
Pull it in to help the sail start turning
Cleat it firmly before you pull the sheet
why: A furling line let go runs wild and tangles on the drum; ease it with a turn on.

q: The boat is head to wind and you are about to hoist the main. Which line must be eased before you pull the halyard?
a: The mainsheet
o: The genoa sheet
The topping lift
The genoa furling line
why: A tight mainsheet holds the boom and leech down, so the sail cannot go up freely.

q: Halfway up, the main fills with wind and the halyard suddenly becomes very heavy. What do you ask the helm?
a: To bring the bow back head to wind
o: To bear away so the sail fills properly
To speed up so the halyard runs easier
To tack so the sail moves across
why: With the bow head to wind the main hangs empty and slides up easily.

q: Why does the instrument show a breeze?
a: It is apparent wind made by the boat's speed
o: A sea breeze is starting to blow
The instrument needs calibrating
The current is dragging the air along
why: Moving through still air at 6 kn makes a 6 kn apparent wind from ahead.

fig.title: Motoring in a flat calm
lines: Wind instrument: 6 kn from dead ahead
Sea glassy, flags ashore hanging limp

q: On this course the genoa keeps collapsing and flapping. Why?
a: The mainsail is blocking its wind
o: The boat is in the no-go zone
The genoa halyard is too tight
The wind is too strong for a genoa
why: Dead downwind the main shades the genoa; goose-wing it or come up a little.

q: How does the boat get to the harbour under sail?
a: By tacking: close-hauled on one tack, then the other
o: Straight at it, with both sheets eased
By gybing back and forth downwind
It cannot: yachts only sail across the wind
why: No boat sails inside the no-go zone, so you zigzag upwind close-hauled.

q: What does the skipper want you to do with the mainsheet?
a: Ease in each gust, pull back in as it passes
o: Keep it cleated so the boat stays steady
Pull in harder in each gust for more power
Ease it right out and leave it there
why: Easing in a gust spills wind and cuts the heel; sheeting back in keeps the drive.

q: What happens to the wind you feel on board?
a: It gets lighter and comes from further aft
o: It gets stronger and comes from further forward
It gets lighter and comes from further forward
It stays the same: only the true wind counts
why: Upwind the boat's speed adds to the wind you feel; downwind it subtracts, and the wind moves aft.

fig.title: Bearing away
lines: From close-hauled to a broad reach
Boat speed rises from 6 to 7 kn

q: The helm gybes onto starboard tack. Which genoa sheet takes the load afterwards?
a: The port sheet: the sails are now to port
o: The starboard sheet: it stays the working one
Both sheets equally until the next tack
Neither: the genoa is furled for every gybe
why: In a gybe the sails cross to the other side, so the other sheet becomes the working sheet.

fig.note: Run on port tack, genoa out to starboard

q: You are trimming the sails. Which wind do they actually feel?
a: The apparent wind, at about 60°
o: The true wind, at about 90°
A mix of both, at about 75°
Whichever is stronger at the time
why: Sails feel the wind on the moving boat: the apparent wind, forward of the true wind.

q: During a tack, the crew on the old genoa sheet lets it go the moment "Ready about" is called, before the boat starts to turn. What is the result?
a: The genoa flaps, the boat loses speed and may stall head to wind
o: The boat turns faster with less load on the sail
Nothing: the timing of the release makes no difference
The genoa backs and pushes the bow through the wind
why: Released early, the genoa stops driving and the boat may stop in irons; let go as the bow passes the wind.
